# Scientific method (conjecture, test, publish, repeat) (`scientific_method`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by empiricism_over_authority, controlled_trial, measurement_quantification, reproducibility_open_publication, fallibilism_provisional_knowledge
- Core idea: To test a claim about nature, state it precisely, work out what you should observe if it is true and if it is false, make the observation or design a comparison that distinguishes the predictions. Measure and record everything including failures, then let others repeat and criticise it. It works because it is a social error-correction process, not because any single person is unbiased. The cheapest way to convince is to predict something in advance that the old view does not predict (which of two pendulums swings faster, whether covered meat breeds maggots) and let the audience watch the outcome. It is a family of habits, not a fixed sequence of steps, and observation sciences (astronomy, anatomy) use it without laboratory experiments.
- Pitfalls:
  - Presenting it as a fixed five-step recipe; real research moves back and forth between guess, test and revision
  - Saying 'science proves things': it eliminates errors and ranks explanations, the result stays open to revision
  - Claiming nobody tested anything before Bacon or Galileo, or that one person (Ibn al-Haytham, Bacon, Galileo) invented it
  - Staging a public demonstration that has not been rehearsed; one visible failure discredits the method and the player
  - Thinking experiments speak for themselves: without a clear rival hypothesis the audience fits any result into the old theory
- History: mesopotamia: c. 750 BC onwards – astronomical diaries: centuries of dated systematic observations used for prediction, without an explicit method of testing causes; china: c. 430–300 BC – the Mozi's 'three tests' of a doctrine (precedent, what people's eyes and ears report, practical benefit); c. 80 AD Wang Chong demands evidence and tests for claims; india: early centuries AD (dating disputed) – Nyaya Sutras classify the valid means of knowledge (perception, inference, comparison, testimony) and rules of debate; greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotle's systematic observation; 3rd c. BC Strato, Archimedes, Alexandrian physicians experiment; 2nd c. AD Ptolemy and Galen report experiments; islamic: early 11th c. – Ibn al-Haytham’s Book of Optics combines geometrical arguments with experiments using light, apertures and screens; europe: 13th c. Grosseteste and Roger Bacon praise experience (how far they experimented is disputed); 1600 Gilbert; 1620 Francis Bacon, Novum Organum; 1632–1638 Galileo; 1660 Royal Society; the word 'scientist' only 1833–1834 (Whewell)
- Read:
  - Ibn al-Haytham, The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham, Books I–III: On Direct Vision (tr. A. I. Sabra, 1989)
  - Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620)
  - David Wootton, The Invention of Science: A New History of the Scientific Revolution (2015)
  - Peter Godfrey-Smith, Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science (2003)
